title: Large models in transportation infrastructure: a perspective
abstract: In late 2022, OpenAI launched ChatGPT and quickly came into the spotlight based on the development of large language modeling technology. ChatGPT is regarded as a new breakthrough in artificial intelligence technology, marking a major advancement in AI technology, stimulating global attention to the application of AI products, and opening up the ‘large model era’ of AI. Large models are also reshaping tasks and achieving impressive results in a wide range of complex downstream tasks (Li et al., 2023). The rapid development of large models provides new solution possibilities for the challenges faced by the transportation infrastructure industry. For the complicated industry specifications, design standards, feasibility study reports, and other textual data, large models can help them to study and integrate to better cope with the complex and changing application scenarios. At the same time, data management and analysis with the help of large language models in the era of big data can facilitate the study and formulation of data standards and processing procedures applicable to the transportation infrastructure industry and promote the scientific application of data in program decision-making and planning. Large models refer to deep neural network models with billions, tens of billions, or even more parameters (Lu, 2019). As shown in Fig. 1, such models are usually pre-trained on massive corpora and can learn complex patterns, linguistic nuances, and semantic relationships, but they are not targeted at a specific downstream task per se but rather gain an understanding of the training data. The application of large models means that the pre-trained large models are used to integrate and migrate the acquired knowledge to each specific downstream task through transfer learning. The training basis of large models The success of large models is inseparable from the application of its key technologies, such as self-attention mechanisms (Vaswani et al., 2017), self-supervised learning (Raffel et al., 2020), prompt engineering, etc. Transformer can model the context relationship in data (text, image, etc.) to obtain rich and effective data representation. Large language models, such as BERT (Devlin et al., 2018) and GPT (Radford et al., 2018), are trained using the Transformer architecture. After the establishment of large models, their downstream applications are based on self-supervised learning. This learning mode avoids the mapping relationship between only fitting data and simple and highly abstract annotations in supervised pre-training and enables the model to learn data representations with rich semantic expression ability and strong generalization ability, so as to better transfer ‘knowledge’ to specific downstream tasks. Hint engineering is regarded as a catalyst to guide the model to output expected answers (Kirillov et al., 2023). Through well-designed inputs, the model can be guided to complete specific tasks, not only in text, but also in modalities, such as images. According to the training data and the type of modality output, large models can be mainly divided into language, visual, and multimodal large models. Language large models learn general features from massive texts, while visual large models focus on giving computers human-like visual processing abilities for understanding, identifying, and processing images and videos. Multimodal large models integrate multi-source data, such as text and images, which is the key to general artificial intelligence (AGI) (Blum and Blum, 2023), and have shown potential in biomedical (Li et al., 2023), scientific research (Beltagy et al., 2019), and other fields. The development of the GPT series models has heralded the era of large pre-trained language models. In addition to the GPT series, companies, such as Google and Microsoft, have also been continuously releasing large models with parameters ranging from hundreds of millions to hundreds of billions. Due to the high dependence of large models on massive computational power and data resources, the research forces are mainly from the industrial community. However, with the release of open-source large models of different parameter sizes by universities, such as Berkeley and Tsinghua, the academic community has also been able to actively participate with limited computational resources. This article summarizes the basic situations of the current mainstream 10 open-source large models, as shown in Table 1 (research time up to April 2024, arranged in ascending order of release time). Representative open source large models basic situation. Representative open source large models basic situation. As shown in Table 1, in the process of the development of open-source large models, the decoder architecture has dominated. The emergent abilities (i.e. abilities that are not explicitly programmed during training but are unexpectedly acquired, which can be understood as the creativity of large models) of the large models based on the decoder architecture with ‘big data + big parameters’ are also more pronounced, highlighting that large models with decoder architecture often possess stronger and more versatile performance. This paper provides a summary of the research status related to large models in the field of transportation infrastructure, as reported in publicly available research papers and patents. The study is organized into four stages: planning and design, project management, operation and maintenance, and safety control. As illustrated in Table 2, the number of literature related to the stage of safety control is the highest, followed by the stages of planning and design and project management. In contrast, the stage of operations and maintenance has the fewest number of literature. This distribution shows the hotspots and focal points of academic research at different stages, while it also highlights some area, particularly operations and maintenance, that may require more research attention, to ensure the overall success and long-term benefits of transportation infrastructure projects. These methodologies and models hold significant guidance and reference value for the establishment of specialized large models within the domain of transportation infrastructure. Literature on large models in transportation infrastructure industry. Literature on large models in transportation infrastructure industry. As depicted in Fig. 2, transportation infrastructure projects encompass a multitude of engineering data, industry standards, and local or national policies, the complexity of which necessitates interdisciplinary research to ensure successful integration (Uddin et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2024). Moreover, the various stages of transportation infrastructure, from planning and design to construction and maintenance, demand a diverse array of specialized skills and knowledge. This integration process relies on the collaborative efforts of a multidisciplinary team comprising designers, engineers, and other professionals, presenting significant challenges for the research and development of large models in transportation infrastructure. The construction process of a large model for transportation infrastructure Large models hold the potential to play a pivotal role in design assistance and inspiration. By analyzing extensive datasets encompassing geographical and economic information (Roberts et al., 2023), these models can aid transportation infrastructure engineers in gaining a more profound understanding of the natural environment and socio-economic conditions of the project site, thereby facilitating the formulation of more rational plans. This is particularly crucial for applications involving environmental data, such as the alignment design of railways and highways, the site selection and planning of stations and bridges, and geospatial analysis, among others. Furthermore, large models can be integrated into the design process to generate design options and recommendations. By incorporating AI-based blueprint review technologies that have been developed over the years, it is possible to achieve intelligent interactions between large language models and engineering drawings (Chen et al., 2022). This capability can be utilized for understanding, querying, and manipulating various architectural domain data, including drawings, models, and specifications, thereby significantly enhancing the efficiency of project design communication. Large models are capable of conducting real-time analysis of various data throughout the project implementation process, thereby offering decision support for project management. Leveraging large language models can assist in the analysis of railway bid documents and the requirement analysis of railway-related software (Abbas et al., 2023; Bashir et al., 2023), which aids in advancing project progress and enhancing the efficiency of project completion. In the realm of operations and maintenance, a comprehensive perspective that considers the viewpoints of designers, civil engineers, and AI programmers can be employed. Utilizing large models for project planning, operational management, design enhancement, and risk mitigation (Rane, 2023) can foster collaboration, effective communication, and the integration of interdisciplinary expertise. In the context of safe control for transportation infrastructure, research on the application of large models mainly involves training and fine-tuning the base models using accident images and textual reports. For instance, by integrating GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020) with stable diffusion (Rombach et al., 2022), and incorporating relevant knowledge about foreign object intrusions on railways, high-quality and highly realistic samples of railway intrusion images can be generated, achieving the goal of preventing railway disasters (Chen et al., 2023). Alternatively, effective action plans can be rapidly generated by including disaster response and planning guidelines in the initial prompts (Goecks and Waytowich, 2023). Similarly, large models can be utilized to analyze aviation safety (Chandra et al., 2023) by mining accident sample data. Looking ahead, the development and research of large models for transportation infrastructure will not be confined to the current domain of professional knowledge querying but will also integrate multimodal technologies. By fine-tuning pre-trained large models toward the field of transportation infrastructure, there is an expectation to create an AIGC (AI-Generated Content) platform specific to this domain, aiming to achieve artificial substitution in engineering processes. Leveraging in-depth industry expertise and relying on AIGC technology, the planning and design of transportation infrastructure is anticipated to achieve intelligent breakthroughs at the forefront. In particular, preliminary design, which relies heavily on industry experience, requires the development of more sophisticated algorithmic models based on professional knowledge. This process entails a longer development cycle and is challenging to realize in the short term. Conversely, construction drawing design is relatively procedural, but it encompasses numerous specialized sub-fields that need to be tackled one by one. In the long term, as model algorithms continue to mature, large models are expected to become involved in various stages, including conceptualization, preliminary design, three-dimensional model output, and drawing review. This integration aims to establish a complete closed-loop system from ‘demand input’ to ‘AI design’, ‘demand feedback’, and ‘design updates’, thereby significantly enhancing design efficiency and optimizing business models. Furthermore, in the field of structural health monitoring, research related to large models barely exists. However, given the robust text data analysis capabilities of large models, there is potential for their application in real-time data analysis of sensors through training and fine-tuning. This could lead to the monitoring of the structural health conditions of transportation infrastructure. Taking the professional intelligent Q&A of railway line selection as a starting point, a professional knowledge Q&A platform case was constructed by combining a large model with a knowledge base to achieve the resolution of issues related to railway line selection. This application not only reflects the practical application value of large models in the field of transportation infrastructure but also demonstrates the potential of artificial intelligence technology in enhancing decision-making efficiency and accuracy. From the perspective of document processing, the working principle of the railway line selection knowledge Q&A platform is shown in Fig. 3. The realization principle of railway line selection knowledge Q&A The case study first examines the Langchain framework and its application in the construction of a professional knowledge base for railway line selection. By employing the data extraction methods of Langchain as well as text embedding techniques, a professional vector data knowledge base for railway lines is established. Subsequently, as shown in Fig. 4, a web-based intelligent Q&A platform for railway line selection is established. It integrates retrieval-enhanced generation technology, text embedding technology, semantic retrieval technology, and prompt engineering. The platform utilizes the BGE embedding model and the ChatGLM2-6B large language model and integrates them into the Q&A system, designing a user-friendly web interface. Langchain+LLM professional Q&A WebUI of railway route selection The case study uploads the document ‘TB 10098-2017 Code for Design of Railway Line’ as the knowledge file and poses questions regarding this specification. The responses obtained from the test are consistent with the content of the provisions recorded in the design specification, as shown in Fig. 5, and are not fabricated. Example of professional Q&A on railway line selection The case study illustrates the strengths of large models in the field of knowledge Q&A. By drawing on this example, knowledge-based Q&A platforms can be established for other specific segments within the field of transportation infrastructure. Looking further into the future, industry-specific algorithms can be integrated into the web platform for invocation, allowing for the modification of algorithm parameters through interaction with the large model. Additionally, a knowledge base can be constructed using engineering case data, enabling the large model to refer to the case database to make suggestions for new tasks. Despite the encouraging achievements made by artificial intelligence in the field of transportation infrastructure, the development of large models within this domain still faces significant challenges, with numerous technical difficulties and issues. The problems shown in Fig. 6 are particularly pronounced. Difficulties and Challenges in developing large models for transportation infrastructure The data within the transportation infrastructure domain encompasses a variety of document types, such as engineering technical forms and design drawings, which include both structured and unstructured elements. To effectively process such data, large models must comprehend their structure and the relationships among them. Documents in the transportation infrastructure field are typically lengthy. As document length increases, large models face challenges in locating key information segments and processing the internal semantic relationships within the documents. Concurrently, there is an urgent need to integrate specialized domain knowledge. The retrieval augmented generator (RAG) architecture (Lewis et al., 2020) is designed to address this challenge, but its integration with the transportation infrastructure context is currently insufficient. In the context of sensitive engineering and topographical information, data privacy protection and security precautions are critical issues for the use of large model technology in the transportation infrastructure sector. It is imperative to implement robust security measures, such as encrypted transmission and enhanced activity monitoring. Additionally, adherence to industry standards and regulations is essential to circumvent potential data privacy and security issues that may arise during the development and application of large models. Due to the nature of large models as black-box models, their internal decision-making processes are hardly interpretable. However, in the context of transportation infrastructure work, explaining the decision-making process of models is not only crucial for overall planning and architectural design stages but also essential for each phase of transportation infrastructure to comply with relevant standards and industry norms. Therefore, the interpretability of the model is equally important. Large models exhibit stability issues, where the model’s output may vary significantly in response to minor changes in the input data, potentially impacting the system’s reliability and consistency. Additionally, managing the connectivity and correlation between different tasks within transportation infrastructure projects represents a significant challenge for large models. Transportation infrastructure projects typically encompass multiple stages, such as pre-feasibility studies, feasibility studies, preliminary designs, and so on. However, large models often tend to provide direct answers, neglecting the records of previous steps and lacking comprehensive and effective explanations and reasoning regarding the future steps and their sequence. As the technology of large models rapidly advances and the quality of their generated content progressively approaches human-level performance, this poses challenges for model evaluation. Currently, the assessment of large models primarily revolves around evaluation metrics (for instance, BLEU and ROUGE are utilized to assess the model’s generative capabilities) and datasets for evaluation. However, in the field of transportation infrastructure, the development and application of large models are still in their infancy, and there is a particular lack of established indicator systems and organized datasets for evaluation. To realize the practical application of large models in transportation infrastructure, the research and development of reliable evaluation methods has become an urgent task. Finally, in the human-centered process of transportation infrastructure construction, decisions at each stage are made by human agents who assume corresponding technical responsibilities. However, with the application of AI technologies, such as large models in the field of transportation infrastructure, the decision-making process will introduce an element of ‘machine will’. Given the large model technology’s capabilities for continuous self-learning and evolution, its decision outcomes may become unpredictable, leading to potential inconsistencies between user intent and model output. In such cases, the attribution of decision-making responsibility and the mechanisms for accountability become complex and difficult to clearly define. The intelligentization of transportation infrastructure largely depends on the integration of diverse AI technologies. Large models, machine learning, deep learning, and big data analytics are all critical components in this field. They work in concert to enhance aspects, such as planning and design, project management, operations and maintenance, and safety control. The integration of large model technology paves the way for the construction of safer, more efficient, and more human-centered transportation infrastructure. The solutions to the difficulties and challenges discussed in Section 4 rely on these artificial intelligence technologies previously mentioned. This includes the standardized construction of professional datasets specific to the transportation infrastructure field, the development of more coherent long-text segmentation techniques, and the creation of more concise and efficient text vectorization technologies. Additionally, it involves the establishment of external information retrieval technologies, evaluation datasets, and assessment metrics. The integration of artificial intelligence technologies centered around large models is imperative. Finally, data privacy protection measures and multi-party accountability mechanisms urgently require enhancement and refinement. Looking ahead, to achieve enhanced specialization, robustness, and generalizability in dynamic, interference, and non-prior complex environments, transportation infrastructure large model technology must make leaps in several areas. These include the transition from purely machine learning models to structurally interpretable models, from offline learning to continuous autonomous learning, and from rote learning to associative inference. Efforts should be concentrated on promoting interdisciplinary innovative research between artificial intelligence, neuroscience, and cognitive science within the field of transportation infrastructure, striving to make breakthroughs in areas, such as interpretability, high security, and low power consumption. By fine-tuning pre-trained large models toward the field of transportation infrastructure, there is an expectation to create an AIGC (AI-Generated Content) platform specific to this domain, aiming to achieve artificial substitution in engineering processes. Leveraging in-depth industry expertise and relying on AIGC technology, the planning and design of transportation infrastructure is anticipated to achieve intelligent breakthroughs at the forefront. In particular, preliminary design, which relies heavily on industry experience, requires the development of more sophisticated algorithmic models based on professional knowledge. This process entails a longer development cycle and is challenging to realize in the short term. Conversely, construction drawing design is relatively procedural, but it encompasses numerous specialized sub-fields that need to be tackled one by one. In the long term, as model algorithms continue to mature, large models are expected to become involved in various stages, including conceptualization, preliminary design, three-dimensional model output, and drawing review. This integration aims to establish a complete closed-loop system from \u2018demand input\u2019 to \u2018AI design\u2019, \u2018demand feedback\u2019, and \u2018design updates\u2019, thereby significantly enhancing design efficiency and optimizing business models. Furthermore, in the field of structural health monitoring, research related to large models barely exists. However, given the robust text data analysis capabilities of large models, there is potential for their application in real-time data analysis of sensors through training and fine-tuning. This could lead to the monitoring of the structural health conditions of transportation infrastructure. Taking the professional intelligent Q&A of railway line selection as a starting point, a professional knowledge Q&A platform case was constructed by combining a large model with a knowledge base to achieve the resolution of issues related to railway line selection. This application not only reflects the practical application value of large models in the field of transportation infrastructure but also demonstrates the potential of artificial intelligence technology in enhancing decision-making efficiency and accuracy. Despite the encouraging achievements made by artificial intelligence in the field of transportation infrastructure, the development of large models within this domain still faces significant challenges, with numerous technical difficulties and issues. The problems shown in Fig. 6 are particularly pronounced. Difficulties and Challenges in developing large models for transportation infrastructure The data within the transportation infrastructure domain encompasses a variety of document types, such as engineering technical forms and design drawings, which include both structured and unstructured elements. To effectively process such data, large models must comprehend their structure and the relationships among them. Documents in the transportation infrastructure field are typically lengthy. As document length increases, large models face challenges in locating key information segments and processing the internal semantic relationships within the documents. Concurrently, there is an urgent need to integrate specialized domain knowledge. The retrieval augmented generator (RAG) architecture (Lewis et al., 2020) is designed to address this challenge, but its integration with the transportation infrastructure context is currently insufficient. In the context of sensitive engineering and topographical information, data privacy protection and security precautions are critical issues for the use of large model technology in the transportation infrastructure sector. It is imperative to implement robust security measures, such as encrypted transmission and enhanced activity monitoring. Additionally, adherence to industry standards and regulations is essential to circumvent potential data privacy and security issues that may arise during the development and application of large models. Due to the nature of large models as black-box models, their internal decision-making processes are hardly interpretable. However, in the context of transportation infrastructure work, explaining the decision-making process of models is not only crucial for overall planning and architectural design stages but also essential for each phase of transportation infrastructure to comply with relevant standards and industry norms. Therefore, the interpretability of the model is equally important. Large models exhibit stability issues, where the model\u2019s output may vary significantly in response to minor changes in the input data, potentially impacting the system\u2019s reliability and consistency. Additionally, managing the connectivity and correlation between different tasks within transportation infrastructure projects represents a significant challenge for large models. Transportation infrastructure projects typically encompass multiple stages, such as pre-feasibility studies, feasibility studies, preliminary designs, and so on. However, large models often tend to provide direct answers, neglecting the records of previous steps and lacking comprehensive and effective explanations and reasoning regarding the future steps and their sequence. As the technology of large models rapidly advances and the quality of their generated content progressively approaches human-level performance, this poses challenges for model evaluation. Currently, the assessment of large models primarily revolves around evaluation metrics (for instance, BLEU and ROUGE are utilized to assess the model\u2019s generative capabilities) and datasets for evaluation. However, in the field of transportation infrastructure, the development and application of large models are still in their infancy, and there is a particular lack of established indicator systems and organized datasets for evaluation. To realize the practical application of large models in transportation infrastructure, the research and development of reliable evaluation methods has become an urgent task. Finally, in the human-centered process of transportation infrastructure construction, decisions at each stage are made by human agents who assume corresponding technical responsibilities. However, with the application of AI technologies, such as large models in the field of transportation infrastructure, the decision-making process will introduce an element of \u2018machine will\u2019. Given the large model technology\u2019s capabilities for continuous self-learning and evolution, its decision outcomes may become unpredictable, leading to potential inconsistencies between user intent and model output. In such cases, the attribution of decision-making responsibility and the mechanisms for accountability become complex and difficult to clearly define. The intelligentization of transportation infrastructure largely depends on the integration of diverse AI technologies. Large models, machine learning, deep learning, and big data analytics are all critical components in this field. They work in concert to enhance aspects, such as planning and design, project management, operations and maintenance, and safety control. The integration of large model technology paves the way for the construction of safer, more efficient, and more human-centered transportation infrastructure. The solutions to the difficulties and challenges discussed in Section 4 rely on these artificial intelligence technologies previously mentioned. This includes the standardized construction of professional datasets specific to the transportation infrastructure field, the development of more coherent long-text segmentation techniques, and the creation of more concise and efficient text vectorization technologies. Additionally, it involves the establishment of external information retrieval technologies, evaluation datasets, and assessment metrics. The integration of artificial intelligence technologies centered around large models is imperative. Finally, data privacy protection measures and multi-party accountability mechanisms urgently require enhancement and refinement. Looking ahead, to achieve enhanced specialization, robustness, and generalizability in dynamic, interference, and non-prior complex environments, transportation infrastructure large model technology must make leaps in several areas. These include the transition from purely machine learning models to structurally interpretable models, from offline learning to continuous autonomous learning, and from rote learning to associative inference. Efforts should be concentrated on promoting interdisciplinary innovative research between artificial intelligence, neuroscience, and cognitive science within the field of transportation infrastructure, striving to make breakthroughs in areas, such as interpretability, high security, and low power consumption.
